newsitem.title: UK: Britain launches Europe's largest wind farm.
newsitem.headline: Britain launches Europe's largest wind farm.

text.p: Britain on Wednesday launched the largest wind farm in Europe to gales of protest from conservationists who say the giant turbines are a blight on the landscape.
The site, on remote sheep-grazing land in mid Wales, will power 25,000 homes in the area.
The 50-metre (164-ft) high turbines are painted white, in stark contrast to the rolling green hills. Their huge three-bladed rotors, whirring in the wind, are 44 metres (144-ft) in diameter.
National Wind Power Ltd, which developed the 26 million pound ($41 million) Carno project with 56 Danish-built turbines, said electricity could now be supplied at half the local cost.
It said opinion polls showed up to eight out of 10 people supported pollution-free windfarms as they harnessed nature and helped to cut acid rain and greenhouse gas emissions.
But environmentalists, eager to balance the need for clean energy against protection of the countryside, said wind farms were being developed at breakneck speed.
The Campaign for the Protection of Rural Wales said the ecology of Welsh peat bogs had been threatened by the Carno project, whose 33.6 megawatt output makes it Europe's largest.
"This is not a cause for celebration but a disaster which should not have been allowed to happen," said Merfyn Williams, director of the conservation group.
"As the massive alien structures have been hauled into our lives, dominating the landscape for miles around, many people have expressed their horror to us," he said.
The Ramblers Association called for a moratorium on government subsidies to wind farms until their environmental impact has been re-evaluated.
"Many of our members are very concerned about the impact of wind turbine development, particularly in wild open upland landscapes," said the group's Welsh spokeswoman Beverley Penney.
Britain now has 31 wind farms providing electricity for around 150,000 homes. Experts say wind power could provide up to 20 percent of Britain's electricity needs.
But industry leaders said the country was lagging behind other Europeans like Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands.

"We enjoy 40 percent of Europe's total wind resource, yet we remain in danger of being left behind in the development of wind power generation worldwide," said Hugh Babington Smith of the British Wind Energy Association.

"With fossil fuels declining, we are urging the government to set a feasible target of 10 percent of electricity from wind by 2025. This would create at least 13,000 new jobs, considerable investment savings and a UK wind industry worth 10 billion pounds," he added.
Its builders say the windfarm will offset the release of 80,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide and 1,200 tonnes of acid rain gases into the atmosphere from conventional power stations.
